One shortcut is to angle the shears and grade both seam allowances in a single cut. That kind of tactile skill can't be handed to a digital agent.
Algorithms and CAD methods exist that automatically choose the parting direction and parting line for cast and molded parts, so an agent can help with planning where to divide a pattern.
Split patterns are made by cutting the wooden pattern into pieces and adding dowels and guide holes. This is physical shop work done with saws, planes and drills.
O*NET lists dividing patterns into sections as a core task for wood patternmakers, alongside shaping and joining the parts with hand tools.

In plants with a DCS (distributed control system), open/close commands for motor-operated valves and drives come from the DCS and run through interposing relays. Every drive still has a local emergency stop pushbutton, so manual field operation remains part of the job.

Automated unit start-up sequences already exist, but they stop at breakpoints where the operator checks the stage and presses a permission button to continue. Many plants still start units in a very manual way.
NERC Reliability Standard PER-003 requires operators in real-time positions that control the Bulk Electric System to hold NERC certification. Licensed humans are expected to be in the control loop.

Test-data platforms already run analysis on measurement data inside the test context. Werum HyperTest Boost connects to JupyterLab, and ZEISS INSPECT automates metrology analysis. Frontier agents with code execution can do the computations and pass/fail checks against a spec end to end.

Under ISO/IEC 17025 and 17020, management must name specific people to authorize and sign test and inspection reports, and accreditation bodies keep lists of these signatories. The analysis can be automated, but a human still has to authorize the result in accredited settings.
The standard requires a review and authorization before results are released, but it does not say how the work behind them is done. That makes the rest of the task digital and open to delegation.

Size, color and weight grading is already automated, but by dedicated conveyor sorters with built-in cameras (ENSCO PROSORT, Key Technology Optyx, Robovision). These are hardware lines, not software agents. A software-only agent could at most classify items from camera images it can reach, while picking up, weighing, moving and sorting the items still has to be done by hand or by the sorting machine.
AI vision is now used for ripeness, color and cluster-size grading, with weight estimated from images. This again runs as purpose-built sorting equipment on the production line.

Official USDA grading certificates need a licensed grader (7 CFR 58.33; for eggs, plant-employee grading is check-graded by a licensed grader). The routine sorting this task describes generally does not need a license, so the accountability barrier is marked false.

Bundles are tied by people or by dedicated strapping machines on conveyor lines (e.g., Signode SGP 3330, which detects, positions and straps bundles). This is mechanical automation, not something a software-only AI agent can do.
In-line squarer-bundlers such as the Mosca MCB-2 align and strap stacks physically. The task means handling products and strapping material by hand or machine, so a physical presence is required.
Automatic bundle strapping systems feed, compress, strap and eject bundles mechanically. The only digital part an AI agent could help with is looking up the prescribed procedure or bundle specs.

Under 49 CFR 232.205, a 'qualified person' must perform the Class I brake test on each train and car at points such as the initial terminal. Under the rule, both the test and the sign-off on it rest with a trained human.

Railinc's eABS tool records the date, time, location, number of cars and qualified person for each brake test. An agent could cross-check whether a test is on record, but the engineer's actual check of brake-pipe pressure and leakage happens in the cab.

Patent filings on automating brake inspection say an inspector usually has to walk the length of the train. They also say automated alternatives such as wireless sensors and camera systems have not been widely adopted.

Vendor material says a grain plant control system (PLC/SCADA) can run motors and route grain from the truck pit to a bin on its own. That logic is fixed automation built into the plant. It is not a general AI agent, and the physical work around the vehicle stays with people.
Truck receiving can be automated with RFID cards, photo eyes and driver touch-screens. This covers the paperwork and data side, but people still have to position the vehicle and open the hopper.
Loadout systems use a PLC to control the conveyor, but an operator still positions the equipment at the start with a handheld control pendant, so a person must be on site.

Vendor pages say AI avatar video tools such as HeyGen can turn a script into branded financial-education presentations with an AI or digital-twin presenter. One vendor-reported case (Samsung Securities) cut video production from 2–3 days to 4–5 hours. These are recorded videos, not live, interactive seminars.

Under FINRA Rule 2210, a registered principal must approve a retail communication before it is used. Study-guide sources (not the rule text itself) say this covers a scripted seminar shown to more than 25 retail investors.

For seminars without a script, FINRA expects firms to supervise the human presenter through written procedures, training and surveillance. That fits a live, person-led session where the advisor answers audience questions and builds client trust.
The core duties are physical: workers climb trees or work from aerial lift trucks, run chainsaws while up in the tree, and use handsaws, pruners and rigging to trim and top branches.

AI-guided chainsaw drones for cutting branches are still a university research project (University of Canterbury, a 5-year grant), not a publicly available software agent. They are also robotics, which the reference technology does not include.
Arborist software only offers tree inventories and marking or tracking trees for pruning. This is a small planning aid, not the cutting and shaping work itself.

ANSI A300 Part 3 covers support system installation: cabling configurations, through-rod and dead-end bracing, guying with ground anchors, and propping. All of it means drilling and fitting hardware in the tree, and no software can do that.

Bracing, guying and propping are hands-on field jobs done at height or at ground anchors. Choosing hardware depends on inspecting the tree, its species and the site. An AI could at most look up the hardware sizing tables in the standard.

To move a tree, workers drive hydraulic spade blades into the soil around the trunk, cut the roots, and box or wrap the root ball. Roots are often pruned 3 to 6 months beforehand. All of this is physical work with machinery on site.
Sources describe root pruning before the dig and preparing the planting hole (breaking up glazed soil, washing soil into gaps) as hands-on work done in the field.

Licensing differs by state. Louisiana requires a license for work on standing trees, while Connecticut does not count removals as licensed arboriculture. So licensing is not a general barrier, and the physical work is what limits AI here.

Older cavity treatment meant physically scraping out decayed wood back to sound wood and then filling the hole with cement, mortar or bricks. This is hands-on work done at the tree, often while climbing.

Arborists working by hand must remove the rotted wood carefully so they don't damage sound wood. Taking out too much weakens the tree, so the job depends on manual skill and judgment on site, which an agent without a body cannot provide.
Current guidance mostly advises against filling cavities. Software could at most help by looking up guidance, which is a very small part of the work.

Mindbody's ZeeZor app pulls per-staff numbers (retail sales, guest retention, service sales) from salon and spa point-of-sale systems. This automates the data side of performance reviews, but nobody has to watch the work being done.

General video tools can watch existing CCTV for staff productivity, uniform or SOP deviations and idle service points. They are sold for restaurants and retail, not built for personal services, and they only work where cameras and access already exist.

A study of AI video misconduct monitoring in restaurants found it can hurt operations. Feedback on individual misconduct such as uniform violations made things worse, so a human supervisor's judgment and delivery of feedback still matter.
Demonstrators physically build and keep up display stations such as tables, carts and booths. They also prepare samples, arrange power and extension cords, and tear down and transport the displays.
AI merchandising tools such as PlanoHero, LEAFIO and Realgram can generate shelf and planogram layouts automatically. That covers only digital layout planning, not physically arranging a demo area.
Employer job descriptions list setting up booths and displays as a core in-person duty, alongside live demos and handing out samples.

H&M's 2025 campaign used photorealistic AI 'digital twins' of real models in some marketing images. The real models kept ownership of their likeness and a revenue share. This replaces the final image, but no agent poses in the model's place.

Zara uses AI to dress models virtually in variations of photos already taken of real models, instead of booking new shoots. It says AI will add to traditional shoots, not replace them, so a human still has to pose for the original shoot.

Zalando reportedly cut campaign lead times from up to 8 weeks to 4 days and costs by about 90% with AI imagery. That replaces the photo output, but the task itself, physically posing at appearances, filming or photo sessions, needs a human body.

Route-sales and DSD apps such as bMobile Route, Pepperi and inSitu can create invoices, process cash, card or check payments, capture signatures and sequence stops. The human driver still carries out the physical handoff and collects the payment in person.
Door-to-door selling means a person physically going to each door. Cities such as Woodinville require each individual seller to hold a peddler's permit, which assumes a human is there.
Peddler licensing usually includes a police background check on each person selling. That is a vetting and permit rule, not a requirement for a human to sign off on delivery or payment.

Good2Go Order Pilot (vendor claim) uses an OpenAI connection to read order emails and attachments. It pulls out page size, page count, quantity, colors, folding and paper, then creates the order in the system automatically.

Docparser offers a printing template that reads job orders and print specs arriving by email, fax or upload. It sends the extracted fields to job management systems, so reading production orders for item types and sizes is already automated.

Fiery JobFlow Pro analyzes job content to identify the job type and routes print jobs to the right presets on its own. Reading and classifying jobs is digital information work with no licensing or sign-off requirement.

FarmHQ's app lets users remotely start and stop irrigation pumps and solenoid valves, set schedules and get fault alerts. This only works where the retrofit hardware is already installed, and it does not cover laying pipe or digging ditches.

WiseConn's irrigation software schedules water by crop stage, soil moisture and weather forecast, and can control valves and pumps remotely. This covers the digital planning and control part of irrigation.

Valley's AgSense/ICON systems allow remote monitoring and control of pivots and pumps, but only through a smart control panel fitted on site. Moving portable pipe, setting siphons and ditch gates, clearing ditches and repairing pumps still has to be done by hand in the field.

Under federal rules, restricted-use pesticides may only be applied by a certified applicator or a trained noncertified person working under that applicator's direct supervision. The applicator must also follow the label and complete equipment training.

The AI spraying products that exist, such as Greeneye's see-and-spray system, are hardware mounted on tractor sprayers. Hand-sprayer work still means a person physically mixing, carrying and applying the chemicals.
Software such as Agremo builds prescription maps from drone or satellite images. That only helps a little with planning where to spray and does nothing for the hand application itself.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l), forklift operators need hands-on practical training and an in-person evaluation on the employer's equipment. Operating material-handling equipment is physical work done in person.

PTx Trimble OutRun automates grain cart movement, but this is robotics built into the tractor, not a software-only AI agent. The cart is still sent to a truck unload zone where a person unloads it by hand.

A Purdue thesis says no existing system can fully automate a combine unloading on the go. Auger control relies on on-machine sensors and actuators, not on any digital system that a software agent could reach.

Dairy feed management software (FeedWatch, Cowconnect, Digi-Star TMR Tracker) adjusts rations and load sizes and tracks loading accuracy. The tractor or loader operator still physically loads the mixer wagon and drives it to deliver the feed.

A University of California study of 26 dairies using feed management software found ingredient loading deviations ranging from about -79% to +22%. The researchers linked this to feeder skill, which shows the core work is physical and done by a human operator.
Topcon TAP FEED software reports operator accuracy and refusals. It supports the human operator who drives the feed equipment but does not replace them.

Barns are cleaned automatically today only by physical robots and scrapers, such as Lely's sensor-guided Discovery scraper that follows pre-programmed routes. These machines are robotics, not software agents, so they fall outside the reference technology.

Existing automatic barn-cleaning systems are autonomous vehicles or scrapers that move or collect manure on predefined tracks and timers. The task is physical manipulation of manure, bedding and equipment.

Vacuum robots like the Discovery 120 spray water and collect manure on solid floors. Even with automation, a machine has to be physically present, so an AI agent with no body can at most look up disinfectant dilutions or cleaning schedules.

Systems that measure log length and diameter and choose where to cut stems (StanForD-based, e.g. Ponsse Opti, Waratah TimberRite) are built into mechanized harvester heads. They are machine control systems, not software agents. A manual faller checks logs on site with a tape and by eye, so an agent can only help, for example by checking photos or measurements a human supplies against the cutting specs.

A Skogforsk 2025 trial found that most shortfalls in bucking results came from errors in the machines' own length and diameter measurements. Even automated systems still need physical control measurements of the actual logs.
California Title 8 §6285 has the faller pump hydraulic tree jacks at the base of the tree and move wedges in progressively as the tree is jacked. This is hands-on manipulation done at the stump.

A NIOSH fatality report recommends that tree fellers use felling wedges along with proper felling technique on trees with back lean. It cites the OSHA 1910.266 requirement to leave enough hinge wood when making the back cut. The task is physical, done during the cut and in a dangerous spot.
Industry sources say jacking needs a competent faller on site who stays in control at the tree. Software agents with no body cannot insert jacks or drive wedges.

O*NET lists 'Place supporting limbs or poles under felled trees to avoid splitting undersides, and to prevent logs from rolling' as a task for Fallers (45-4021.00). It is hands-on work with heavy material done on site in the woods.
A NIOSH fatality report describes a faller killed when an unstable log pivoted downslope while being bucked. Keeping logs from rolling is physical, on-site safety work that software cannot do.
Michigan's logging rules tell fellers to cut from the uphill side when a tree may slide or roll. This shows that handling logs depends on physical judgment at the site.

How to modify grout mixing is set by each manufacturer's data sheet and by ANSI A108.10, for example water limits, pot life, discarding stiff batches and site-mix ratios. An AI agent can look these up and turn them into adjusted procedures for the helper.

Getting a consistent batch depends on hands-on mixing technique and on judging consistency on site. Sika even recommends having the same person mix every batch, so a human has to do and judge the physical work.

Premixed grouts follow separate standards (ANSI A118.19 and A108.22). Picking the right procedure for each material is an information task that software can support, but no licence or sign-off by a human is required.
Pandrol sells petrol and hydraulic rail drills that a worker clamps onto the rail and runs by hand on the track to bore bolt holes for fishplates, so the task is done in person with a physical tool.

Patents describe a robot on a maintenance vehicle that positions a rail drill using sensors. This automation needs robotics, which the bodiless software agents in the reference technology do not have.
ROBEL and FANUC have rail-repair robots on track wagons as prototypes. I found no deployed autonomous rail-drilling system that a software-only agent could run.

The search found no AI tool that diagnoses tractor wiring faults on its own. The closest tools are AI troubleshooting and interactive wiring navigators for heavy machinery (Tweddle Troubleshooter/TRACER-X) and industrial panels (INTrouble). These guide a human technician; they do not do the meter testing, soldering or part replacement.

Commercial repair software adds interactive wiring diagrams that link components to location, testing and replacement procedures. This is information support only: a technician still has to be at the machine with meters and hand tools.

Farm equipment mechanics generally need no licence. Agricultural technician certification is voluntary in most Canadian provinces and only compulsory for heavy-duty work in some, such as Alberta. The search did not check US state rules or dealer certification programs.

AI diagnostic tools for appliance technicians, such as Marcone AI (built on OpenAI/ChatGPT) and aiventic, guide technicians step by step through troubleshooting and help identify parts. The human technician still does the diagnosis and repair.
An industry guide describes AI appliance-repair tools as decision-support aids for technicians, not definitive diagnostic solutions, especially for older equipment.

Most US states require no general appliance-repair licence. Exceptions include EPA Section 608 certification for refrigerant work and California's registration and licence rules for larger repairs, so licensing is generally not what requires a human for this task.

VendSoft lists automatic commission calculations for locations and route drivers, plus commission statements and sales-by-location reports. These cover the invoicing and account-settlement steps. The source is a vendor listing, so the claims are unverified.

Nayax telemetry and cashless systems send real-time sales and machine data, so an agent can reconcile expected takings and prepare settlements without visiting the machine. The source is vendor marketing.

Taking coins and bills out of machines is physical work done on site. No search in this check showed that an AI agent can do it. This part is my judgement, and it accounts for most of the task's time.

Automatic pressing plants, like rotating carousels that press trousers with steam or hot air, are physical machines that cut down on operators. That automation comes from the machinery, not from a software agent.
Commercial automatic shirt presses still need an operator on site to load the garment and press two start buttons at once for safety. This is hands-on work.

A low-authority job-risk site credits the gains in this job to automated buck presses, tunnel finishers and robotic loaders. All of these are physical robots or machines, and none is software reachable by an AI agent.

Threading a machine is entirely hands-on: you raise the presser foot and needle with the hand wheel, then pass thread through the guides, the take-up lever, the needle eye and the presser foot. An AI agent that can only use software cannot do any of this.

Threading guides describe a manual sequence of steps that depend on the specific machine model. The only digital help is a threading diagram or manual, which a worker would already have, so AI adds little.
Common threading guides list only physical steps, such as snapping the thread into guides and pulling it through the presser foot. None of these steps can be done through software.

Stoll's knitelligence software covers design through production. Its Stoll-autocreate tool turns artwork into a knitting program, so part of reading a pattern and deriving a program is already automated. A job-risk analysis notes that the physical changeover on the machine is still done by people.

Weaving CAD tools such as WeavePoint, Pointcarre Dobby and DNC.GARM.DOBBY generate threading, treadling, tie-up and lift plans and produce spec sheets and loom-readable files. An agent could read these documents and work out setup parameters from them.

No source shows AI taking a mill's written specification and producing a complete loom setup. Most tools start from a drawn or image design. Checking physical fabric samples and talking with floor supervisors still needs a person on site.

StitchDesk is listed as an AI system for upholstery shops that automates fabric yardage calculations along with inventory and invoicing. This comes from a directory listing, and the features were not checked independently.

Fabric yardage calculators take piece sizes, roll width, piece count and allowances and return both the exact cut yardage and the amount to buy. An agent can repeat this from the measurements on a work order.

A supplier's furniture-shape yardage chart is only a general guide because real pieces vary. Getting an accurate estimate still means measuring or inspecting the workpiece, and only a human in the shop can do that.

O*NET lists this as a core task for Model Makers, Wood (51-7031.00). It means fitting and joining wood parts by hand with glue, nails, dowels, bolts and screws. This is physical work that an agent with no robotics cannot do. At most, AI could help by planning joinery or assembly order, which is a small share of the time.
The duties around this task are also hands-on: trimming and sanding surfaces by hand, marking assembly details on parts, and finishing models with shellac, lacquer or wax.

Wood patternmakers build unit or sectional patterns for sand-casting molds. This is shop-floor work with no licence or sign-off required. The barrier is that it must be done physically, not any legal rule.

Machine-learning anomaly detection on refinery process telemetry is already in use. Kaspersky MLAD was piloted on TANECO's CDU-VDU-7 unit, and a 2026 preprint describes adaptive online monitoring with LLM-assisted fault diagnosis, so the control-room part of monitoring can be largely automated.

Operator rounds mean physically walking the unit to read local gauges and tank levels, check valve positions and pumps, and notice leaks, noise, vibration and hot spots. These are physical sensing steps a software agent cannot do.

Under OSHA's PSM rules, operator rounds in covered processes check pressure, temperature, tank levels and samples against operating limits. Responsibility for these checks sits with trained operators and the employer's procedures, not with a personal licence or sign-off.

ASTM D4007 sets out a hands-on lab method for measuring water and sediment in crude oil with a centrifuge. Someone has to physically prepare the sample and run the centrifuge. The results are used to work out net volumes for sales and custody transfer.

Inline BS&W and watercut monitors already check crude quality automatically in LACT custody-transfer systems. This is fixed process hardware, though, not an AI agent. A software agent could at most help with calculations or record-keeping.

LACT parts and how they operate, including automatic sampling, are covered by API MPMS standards (Chapter 8.2 for samplers). These are industry standards, not licensing rules that require a particular person to sign off.

Removing rust on a ship means a person physically holds and runs pneumatic needle scalers (1.3–3.2 kg, 6–7 bar, 101–109 dB(A)) against steel decks and hulls. A software-only agent has no way to do this.
Needle scalers for shipyards are sold as hand tools with flexible needles that a person guides over uneven surfaces and projections. The task is manual work, not a digital process.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l) says only trained, employer-certified operators may run powered industrial trucks such as forklifts. Training includes hands-on practice and an evaluation of the operator in the workplace, so the task is physical and a trained human must be accountable for it.

Automating this transfer work takes physical robots (AMRs and autonomous forklifts that move parts between machines). The software-only agents used as the reference technology here are not robots, so they cannot move the materials themselves.

ABB's Flexley Stack F712 autonomous forklift (2026) shows that robotics does this work in factories, not language-model agents. A software agent could at most help with dispatch or WMS/MES scheduling, which is a small part of the job.
Agentic QA tools from 2026 plan, generate, run and repair software tests on their own, with humans setting goals and reviewing results. These claims come mostly from vendors.
Closed-loop LLM agents such as AgentDV generate hardware (RTL) testbenches, run simulations and refine them using coverage feedback. This work is simulation-based.

Agent-driven hardware-in-the-loop tests run on physical devices, and code that compiles can still fail on real hardware because of timing or peripheral behavior. Someone still has to set up the hardware, and a human has to validate the results.

AI tools for wheel-throwing feedback exist only as research prototypes (a CMU mixed-reality system using computer vision and LLMs). Researchers note that ceramics is embodied and its tacit knowledge is hard to pass on, so an AI can at most support a human teacher.

Studio job postings for pottery instructors ask for hands-on wheel-throwing and hand-building skill, prior teaching experience and a background check. The work is in-person demonstration and guidance in the studio.
Hiring sources ask for experience and a practice record, not a licence. Postings in the US and UK show no legal certification requirement for pottery instructors.

MSHA fatality reports describe workers who were killed while shovelling or cleaning conveyor spillage. Both blamed failures in safe spillage-removal procedures, such as not de-energizing and blocking the belt. This shows the task is hands-on physical work inside the conveyor area.

MSHA housekeeping standards (30 CFR 56/57.20003) require operators to keep work areas, including conveyor walkways, free of spillage. The requirement is met by removing material physically, not through documents or digital systems.

Underground coal spillage under belts and at transfer points builds up and becomes a fire or explosion hazard. Dealing with it takes physical cleaning on site underground, where a software-only agent cannot act.

Applied environmental research often includes hands-on field and lab work: soil and groundwater sampling, pilot tests, remediation monitoring, and lab tests of water quality. An agent cannot do these steps itself.

LLM multi-agent frameworks published in 2026, such as OpenAqua for early-stage water treatment train design and LLM agents for wastewater plants, already do the digital parts: literature retrieval, design options, modeling and optimization.
O*NET 19-2041.00 lists this task next to doing research or investigations to identify and abate pollutant sources. It is a research role with no required licensed signature for the research itself.

Certified CT explosive detection systems already use an automated detection algorithm that makes a yes-or-no alarm decision. A screener reviews the flagged objects on screen and can override the alarm and clear the bag. Bags the screener does not clear go to secondary inspection: they are opened or swabbed for explosive traces.
The National Academies describe on-screen alarm resolution as a human step: the screener either clears the alarm or sends the bag on for more inspection. Each false alarm costs staff time.

Under 49 CFR 1544.207, TSA or its contractors must inspect property before it is loaded. Subpart E sets qualification rules for anyone who performs a screening function, so a qualified human screener must make and own the decision.

In in-line systems, conveyors move checked bags through EDS machines. Bags that alarm are routed to resolution rooms or to a secondary area, where officers search them by hand. The automation that exists is conveyor and EDS hardware, not a software agent, and the searches are done by people on site.
TSA describes an image review step in a control room. Bags that need a physical search are then conveyed to an inspection area and searched by officers under CCTV.

Under 49 U.S.C. 44901, screening of passengers and property must be done by federal government employees, with listed exceptions (the current text cites section 44920), and supervised by uniformed TSA personnel.

AI tools already turn SOPs into training modules, videos and assessments. In regulated settings, subject-matter and quality reviewers still edit and approve the output before it is assigned, so the AI does not author unsupervised.
21 CFR 211.25 requires GMP training to be given by qualified individuals on a continuing basis. A qualified person must run and be accountable for the training.
Guidance for AI-generated GxP training calls for traceability back to the source SOP version, audit trails and human validation of all AI-generated content.

Commercial modeling tools such as OLI ScaleChem, OLI Corrosion Analyzer and Nalco Geomizer predict scaling and corrosion risk in geothermal plants and are used to design inhibitor programmes. An agent could run these tools or similar chemistry models and draft the selection analysis.

A DOE-funded project says no current tool accurately predicts both scaling and corrosion, and that turning model output into practical action still needs a separate advisory layer. Expert judgement and site validation therefore remain essential.

Corrosion control systems are generally designed and installed by, or under the direction of, a qualified person such as a PE or an AMPP/NACE specialist. Implementation means physical installation, monitoring coupons and site work, which needs human sign-off and presence.

Plant startup and shutdown are still done mostly by hand. AI-agent control of startup and shutdown is at the research stage, mainly reinforcement-learning work on nuclear plants, with no commercial control-system deployment found. The researchers also say it is hard to retrofit onto existing plants.

Shutting a boiler down for maintenance means physically isolating every energy source (electrical, fuel, steam and water pressure) and applying lockout/tagout devices under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147. When several crews work on the same equipment, a group lockout is used.
Boiler operator licensing comes from state and local rules, not OSHA. Employers remain liable for unsafe conditions. OSHA cited a biomass plant in New Hampshire for lockout/tagout training failures.

Hydro O&M platforms such as GE Vernova APM and Andritz DiOMera already offer ML-based anomaly detection, predictive maintenance alerts and a CMMS module for digitising maintenance work. An agent could use these to plan maintenance, schedule work, track work orders and write reports.

Maintenance on generation equipment falls under OSHA 1910.269(d) hazardous-energy control (lockout/tagout). That rule requires on-site isolation, verification and authorization by qualified people, so a human has to oversee the work and sign off on safety.

Remote or unmanned hydro sites still need on-site servicing and coordination with the system operator for energy isolation. Supervising installations means being physically present to direct crews and contractors.

Warranty claims software now includes AI agents that handle claims end to end, with claim scoring and anomaly detection. These products are generic and built for the OEM side, not wind-specific, which suggests the paperwork and tracking parts of the task can be automated.

In wind, warranty management relies on continuously collecting turbine data (such as SCADA and condition monitoring) and filing claims throughout the warranty period. These are digital steps an agent could carry out.

Turbine-by-turbine physical inspections at end of warranty, plus filing on time with OEMs, decide whether claims get honoured. Field crews do the physical work, and commercial negotiation with OEMs stays with a human.

RACER is a parametric remediation cost tool used by agencies and consultants. It calculates technology quantities, localizes unit costs and applies markups, so the cost-estimating sub-step is already automated and can be run through software.

New York remediation feasibility study reports carry a licensed Professional Engineer's certification under 6 NYCRR Part 375, and NYSDEC has sent back a report that was missing it. A human must still sign.
Texas rules list a feasibility study as a required part of a remedial investigation. These studies are formal regulatory documents that the agency reviews.

Commercial AI assistants such as dbForge AI Assistant already find inefficient or missing indexes, generate indexing scripts, explain the causes of SQL errors and suggest fixes. That covers the main technical sub-steps of answering a support question.
Practitioners say AI SQL optimization works well as an assistant but still needs human checking and testing before anyone trusts it on production systems. So a human review step remains.
A developer at a company with no DBA used AI to fix SQL Server performance problems. This shows AI can stand in for some of the support a senior database person would give.

AI agent tools such as Powerdrill Bloom and multi-agent slide generators turn raw files (Excel, CSV, PDF) into reports and presentation decks. That covers the drafting part of reports and slides. One analysis notes that much of the time saved goes into checking and refining what the AI produces.

Vendor tools say they can process raw data, run statistical analysis and produce slides ready to present. These claims come from the vendors and have not been independently tested on engineering-grade results.

State rules on engineer seals, such as Florida's, require a licensed PE to sign and seal reports that contain professional engineering work. Most nanosystems R&D and program-review reporting falls outside these rules, so this is not a typical legal barrier for this task.

FutureHouse's Robin multi-agent system generates hypotheses, proposes experiments and interprets experimental data, which are the design and interpretation sub-steps. FutureHouse says its designs are not yet detailed enough to execute without human lab work, and the RPE-cell experiments were run by humans.

Secondary reports say OpenAI and Ginkgo Bioworks had GPT-5 design about 36,000 cell-free protein synthesis experiments that robots in a cloud lab carried out, with the results fed back to the model. This shows execution can be closed-loop only where robotic cloud-lab access exists.

An Active Site study found that AI help did not significantly change novices' ability to complete a complex wet-lab virus-production workflow. Hands-on bench execution and oversight still depend on people.

Skin Analytics' DERM holds an EU Class III CE mark to make skin-lesion decisions on its own. A UK hospital trust says it uses DERM to discharge patients with benign lesions without a dermatologist's input, so lesion-image diagnosis can be delegated. Both sources are promotional and independent validation is limited.

In the US, the FDA-authorized AI skin cancer device DermaSensor only assists clinicians. Its output reads 'investigate further' or 'monitor' and is not a standalone diagnosis, so a licensed clinician still makes the diagnosis and treatment decision.

A JAMA Dermatology review found that none of 41 consumer dermatology apps had FDA approval and that their performance was inconsistent. Without a licensed human in charge, AI diagnosis and treatment carry liability and reliability risks.

Lab scheduling software already assigns staff automatically by credentials, competencies and bench requirements, and fills open shifts. AI workforce tools forecast lab demand, but a human still reviews their recommendations before schedules change.
Rostering software for pathology labs coordinates benches, on-call shifts, couriers and collection centres, so the main sub-steps of coordinating assignments are already done in software.

CLIA cytology rules cap screening at 100 slides per 24 hours and require each person's workload limit to be reassessed at least every 6 months, with documentation. Surveyors cite labs for gaps, so a qualified human supervisor stays accountable for workload assignments.
Consumer labor apps such as Freya and ONA already coach breathing through each contraction and play relaxation audio, so software can deliver the breathing and music parts.
Continuous labor support is mostly hands-on, in-person work: massage, warm baths and encouraging the mother to move. Its benefits are tied to a supportive human being present.
Hydrotherapy, touch and massage, and movement and positioning are effective comfort measures, and all of them need someone physically there to carry them out.

A leak test has to be done on the physical endoscope before cleaning or disinfection. The scope is pressurized and the tester watches for a pressure drop, so it has to be connected and handled by hand, either dry in air or wet under water.

Automated leak testers exist (Olympus ALT-Pro, Medivators Veriscan LT) and cut down on operator subjectivity, but they are physical devices. A person still has to connect the scope and run the test. A software agent has no way to do this.

Automated leak-test systems reduce variation between users, but staff still have to set up the equipment and inspect it. An AI agent could only help with checklists, logging results and looking up manufacturer instructions.

AI articulation apps such as Sara for SLP, SpeechLP and TikTalk generate practice sets, listen to speech, find phoneme errors, give real-time feedback and report progress to SLPs. They support drill practice between sessions, but the SLP programs and directs them. These claims come from the vendors and press coverage, and I did not check them independently.

Under ASHA's scope of practice, SLPAs do tasks that a certified or state-credentialed SLP prescribes, directs and supervises. Training, credentialing and supervision requirements govern the role, and state rules decide the binding details.

A state guideline defines direct, immediate and indirect supervision for SLPAs. For some direct work with clients and families, such as with medically fragile infants, immediate supervision is required. That points to in-person interpersonal care, though teletherapy also exists.

Loss prevention store audits are on-site walkthroughs. The auditor checks the entrance, stockroom, CCTV, EAS tags, display locks, fitting rooms and receiving dock security, and watches staff follow procedures in person. An agent without a body cannot do this.

Audit templates cover about 60 checks across physical security, cash/POS controls, inventory shrink and corrective actions. They also include reviewing earlier findings and incidents, which is digital prep work an agent can do.
AI tools already group POS exceptions, assign risk scores, link transactions to video and flag shelf and inventory mismatches. This covers the data-analysis part of finding problem areas.

Vendor AI video analytics running on existing CCTV say they can flag unauthorized removal of goods, shipment mismatches, loitering and entry into restricted zones at loading docks and in warehouses. This covers much of the work of watching and reviewing footage. These are vendor claims and were not independently checked.

Covert surveillance in loss prevention depends on hidden cameras built into walls or ceilings or disguised as objects such as exit signs, so someone must physically install them. This physical setup, along with in-person stakeouts and undercover observation, is outside what a bodiless agent can do.
A practitioner post on an industry forum says covert cameras are widely used in retail loss prevention to watch areas the everyday camera system cannot see. This is an anecdotal account, not a study.

Slicing fruit, vegetables, desserts or meats means a worker handles knives or slicers and the food itself. Food Code 3-301.11 governs how workers physically touch ready-to-eat food, which an agent with no body cannot do. It only requires utensils or gloves and does not require a licensed human to carry out the task.
Cut fruits and vegetables and sliced deli meats count as ready-to-eat foods. They must be handled with deli tissue, tongs or single-use gloves, which are all physical hygiene steps at the station.

The FDA's rationale is that touching ready-to-eat food with bare hands can spread foodborne illness, so the task depends on hands-on food handling. A software agent could only help at the edges, for example with prep lists or portion guides.

DOE Weatherization Job Aid 20-1, which follows Standard Work Specifications 5.0107.1, has the installer seal the ducts and then fasten the insulation mechanically with wire or twine. The installer also tapes the vapor-retarder seams and must avoid compressing the insulation. All of these are hands-on steps done at the duct.

Job Aid 20-2 has the installer wrap metal fittings such as boots and elbows separately with vapor-retarder duct wrap. It also requires at least R-8 on new flex duct and support for ducts exposed in unconditioned spaces, which means physical work in attics and crawlspaces.
The ROCKWOOL ductwrap installation guide describes cutting, wrapping and fastening the wrap by hand. Software or AI can't do these steps; an agent could only look up specs or R-value requirements.

BUCHI's NIR-Online sensor measures quality parameters such as water, acid value and glycerol continuously in biodiesel production. Once a plant has these sensors installed, the monitoring is done by instruments and software, so an agent could watch and interpret the data.

Producers hesitate to install in-line analysis because the systems are complex and costly to maintain. Many plants still rely on sampling and lab or at-line testing, which needs a person on site to collect and handle the samples.

The BQA 1000 is an at-line analyzer for feedstock and B100 quality. Someone has to draw a sample and feed it to the instrument, so the measuring step is physical. An agent could only help by logging the readings and flagging values outside spec.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.22, employers must keep workrooms and walking-working surfaces clean, orderly and as dry as feasible, free of spills and leaks, and inspected regularly. Meeting this takes physical cleaning on site, which an agent without a body cannot do.

Housekeeping guidance focuses on hands-on work such as cleaning up spills, clearing clutter and preventing slips, trips and falls. An AI agent could only help with peripheral parts like checklists or logging.
Housekeeping duties also come from the flammable liquids standard (1910.106) and combustible dust guidance, and these too are met by physically cleaning the site.
Pactum's AI negotiates supplier contracts on its own, mostly long-tail and low-value deals for companies like Walmart and Maersk. Strategic negotiations are still largely handled by humans.

In Nashville, the Metro Council must approve by resolution any solid waste collection or disposal contract worth $500,000 or more a year, and an authorized official executes it. A human sign-off is therefore required.
In Monroe, the city council selects the solid waste collection contractor and approves its contract and any addenda.

Indonesia's grid code requires automatic generation control on plants above 5 MW. Since 2017 many geothermal plants follow load according to the dispatcher's daily plan. Because reservoirs differ, the AGC mode has to be chosen carefully to protect production wells. Software already handles the routine load following, but people still have to judge the reservoir and steam constraints.

At PLN/Pertamina geothermal plants, the Yokogawa control system automates startup and shutdown sequences, which cuts down on operator intervention. Setpoint and control changes are made through the control screens, so an agent with that access could in principle make them.

NERC's PER-003 certification rule covers reliability coordinators, transmission operators and balancing authorities. A 2008 NERC drafting document says certification of generator operators was left out of it. No licence rule was found that requires a human to make geothermal plant adjustments.

Psychiatric institutions began controlled trials of ambient AI scribes that draft notes for clinicians, including nurses, in August 2026. This shows AI can draft documentation, but clinicians still review it. No product specific to inpatient aide or nursing notes was found.

Psychiatric hospital records must show the degree and intensity of treatment, and surveyors cite missing 15-minute observation-check records. These records come from staff who observe patients in person on the unit.
Under CMS rules for psychiatric hospital records (42 CFR 482.61), entries must be authenticated by an accountable author. A human has to observe the patient and sign the note.
Cleaning food-contact surfaces is hands-on work: pre-scrape, wash, rinse, sanitize, then air dry. A software agent with no robotic body cannot do any of these steps.
Under the Food Code, all surfaces must be washed and rinsed, and food-contact surfaces must also be sanitized. All of this is physical work done in the kitchen.
Food-safety software such as Xenia only covers digital side work like cleaning schedules and checklists. The cleaning itself still has to be done by a person.
Caring for children with disabilities involves hands-on physical help: tube feeding, suctioning, toileting, diapering, and moving or positioning the child.
Supported child care workers help with feeding, lifts and transfers, grooming and toileting, and carry out exercise and mobility care plans.
AI is used for side tasks such as drafting support or IEP plans and giving children learning or schedule aids. A human still reviews the plans, and the people involved decide the services.

Funeral home software such as Kindred, FuneraliQ+ and Osiris already includes built-in accounting, financial performance reports and QuickBooks integration, and some products add AI assistants. Most of this is vendor marketing, and I found no independent test of how well the AI insight features work.

General AI agents (ClickUp, Taskade) are sold for profit-and-loss analysis and cost-reduction planning. They flag costs that look too high, compare spending with industry norms and watch budgets for overruns. The same sources say humans still need to review nuanced, sector-specific cases. No independent case studies were found.

Reviewing internal performance data is a management analysis task. It needs no physical presence, and no licence or signature rule requires a human to do it. The agent's output still has to be checked by the manager, who knows local context such as families, staff and how services run on the ground, before anyone acts on it.

Community health workers hand out flyers in person, door to door: they leave them on homes and car windshields and give them out at community events. An agent with no body cannot do this core activity.

Automated SMS and AI-driven outreach already reach targeted families digitally. In one trial, a GPT-4o phone agent booked visits. This means agents can handle the digital side of distribution, such as texts, emails and social posts, plus list targeting and logistics.

AI can draft health-education texts, but researchers found that expert review is essential for accuracy and appropriate language. This supports the view that agents help with preparation but do not carry out the whole task.

A 2026 preprint used automated PubMed retrieval and NLP to organize the music therapy literature. The authors say AI should support retrieval and professional judgment, not replace clinical expertise, so an agent can do the search and synthesis but the clinician still applies the findings.

Some US states require music therapists to hold MT-BC board certification and a state license. A credentialed human is therefore responsible for clinical decisions about using research-based interventions with clients.
Turning research into practice includes delivering and adjusting music interventions in live sessions with clients, which needs physical presence and a therapeutic relationship.

Guiding is mostly done in the field: the guide leads clients through terrain, shows them stalking, calling and shooting techniques, and keeps them safe. In many jurisdictions anyone guiding for pay must be a licensed human who meets age and first aid/CPR requirements, passes a background check and a written law exam, and is sponsored by an outfitter.
Montana's Board of Outfitters requires guides to be licensed, hold current first aid certification and be sponsored by a licensed outfitter.

Existing AI tools only help with background learning, such as IHEA's experimental Scout assistant for hunting regulations and apps that recommend strategy. They do not teach in the field, so the parts an agent could take over are mainly prep materials and answering questions.

Home Depot's AI Blueprint Takeoffs tool (Nov 2025) produces a full material list and quote for single-family projects from plans, but a Pro team reviews the scope before the list is final. That shows the work can be partly delegated with human review.
Commercial AI takeoff tools such as Attentive.ai (vendor claims 98%+ accuracy), Autotakeoff and Beam AI automatically pull material quantities and dimensions from multi-page blueprints.
Most US states do not license carpenters directly, and no licence requires a human to sign off on reading plans or doing material takeoffs.

Leak testing means hands-on work. The technician isolates and seals the system, connects a nitrogen tank and regulator to a service port, pressurizes it to a set test pressure, watches the gauge for 30-60 minutes or longer, and brushes soap solution on joints to find the leak. All of this needs physical presence.

Under EPA Section 608 (40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F), anyone who attaches hoses and gauges to measure pressure, or adds or removes refrigerant, must be a certified technician. Uncertified apprentices need close supervision by a certified technician.
Under F-Gas rules, engineers must be able to show that leak checks were done before and after charging. That puts the record-keeping and responsibility on a qualified human.

Courier AI agents handle the digital side of the work, such as dispatch, scheduling and pickup intake. A human driver still has to drive and carry the items, and the agent can only plan or coordinate the errand.
Courier support agents take pickup requests and quotes and then pass them to human dispatch. That covers only the coordination part of the errand.
Agent tools can schedule pickups through an API, which speeds up the planning step. Collecting and dropping off mail and packages still needs physical presence, and agents have no robotics.

Telematics platforms such as Motive, CalAmp CrashBoxx and Mojio, combined with RapidSOS, detect crashes automatically. They alert fleet managers and send location and severity data to dispatch or 911. Some workflows still depend on a human to verify the crash or make a phone call.
CalAmp CrashBoxx gives fleet operators a first notice of loss within seconds. It uses context to filter out false alarms, so part of the reporting job is already automated.

The FMCSA bans commercial drivers from using hand-held phones while driving, but two-way radios are exempt. No law requires a human to make these reports. The driver's on-scene observation is still the main input.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l), only trained and authorized operators may run powered industrial trucks. The employer must evaluate each operator in the actual workplace and certify the training. Operators are re-evaluated at least every 3 years.

Autonomous forklifts exist, such as Walmart's FoxBot units at four distribution centers and Fox Robotics, which Symbotic acquired. They are dedicated robotic hardware, though, which is outside the reference technology because it has no physical body. A software agent cannot drive a standard forklift.

Forklift work means physically steering and lifting loads in a warehouse. The only digital parts an agent could handle are small ones, such as checking a pick list or a work order on a scanner or WMS screen.

MEX CMMS says its AI scheduler reviews all open work orders and assigns each to a technician by skills, trade and availability. Supervisors can preview and edit the schedule before applying it, so a human still reviews the result.
JLL describes Corrigo CMMS as using AI scheduling to assign tasks automatically by priority, technician skills and availability.

This overview of AI-powered CMMS describes AI scheduling as an assistant that recommends assignments by urgency, location and expertise, with final decisions left to human planners. It cites no licensing rule that requires a human to sign off on crew schedules.

Most of the work happens on site: walking the scene, taking measurements from fixed points with tape, total station or a laser scanner, and drawing a rough sketch. An agent with no body cannot do this. Drawing the final diagram afterwards can be done in software that takes scanner point clouds and manual measurements as input. FARO Zone, for example, is sold as a replacement for hand-drawn sketches, so an agent could plausibly draft the final diagram from field data.

For a sketch to be admitted in court, it must name who made the rough and final versions and show case identifiers, scale, a north arrow, and evidence numbers that match the evidence log. The final version must also reflect the rough sketch. This means a human has to check and take responsibility for it.

Courts admit scene diagrams and laser-scan products based on testimony from the person who took the measurements: that the measurements are accurate and that the equipment was validated and calibrated. A human has to vouch for the work.

Running an excavator or backhoe without an operator needs robotic retrofit hardware installed on the machine, such as Built Robotics' Exosystem with radar, 360° cameras and GPS, or Bedrock Operator. That is physical robotics, which the reference agent does not have. A software-only agent cannot work the machine's controls.

OSHA has no general licence for heavy-equipment operators. 29 CFR 1926.20(b)(4) and 1926.21(b)(2) require employers to let only people qualified by training or experience operate equipment. This is an employer training duty, not a sign-off that must be done by a licensed person.
The task means working the machine controls on a job site and watching the surroundings in real time. Apart from small planning or locate lookups, it is entirely physical.

Software MRI simulators (Corsmed, ScanLabMR) already provide virtual scanner training with built-in course creation, grading and progress tracking, so the didactic and protocol-practice parts of instruction can be handed to software.
Hands-on training for positioning, coils and patient comfort uses physical mock scanners or real equipment, so a person has to be physically present to demonstrate and correct.

ARRT requires clinical competencies such as MRI safety, positioning and quality control to be verified by an ARRT-registered MR technologist or another qualified person, so a human has to sign off on trainee competence.

Hospital room disinfection is done by people with their hands, sometimes helped by dedicated UV-C robots. UV robots are hardware, not software AI agents, and the vendor itself calls them a supplementary device that assists cleaning staff.
A 2025 hospital study found that UV-C robots and hydrogen peroxide vapor methods fall short on shaded areas and surface contamination, so physical wiping is still needed.
Even an autonomous UV disinfection robot needs a physical platform to clean a room, which a software-only agent does not have.

The bedpan procedure is hands-on work: gloving, placing a barrier, positioning the pan under the patient, then emptying it into a toilet or graduated cylinder and recording output. Only the recording step is digital.

Debilitated, obese or post-surgical patients often need two or more staff to move on or off the pan. Forcing the pan under a patient risks friction injury to the skin, which takes careful physical handling.
State nurse aide checklists test this as a physical skill. Toileting is offered every two hours and calls for sensitive, therapeutic communication because incontinence is embarrassing for patients.
O*NET lists changing soiled linens, drapes and cubicle curtains as a hands-on orderly task, alongside collecting soiled linen and trash.
Florida's hospital rules require soiled linen to be collected in a way that limits the spread of microbes. This is physical handling done under infection-control procedures.
A York hospital (UK) guideline sorts linen into used, soiled and infected, and each type needs physical bagging and handling at the bedside.

Hospital PAR software such as Cognosos ProPAR tracks room-level stock against PAR thresholds, sends alerts and builds pick lists for the staff who restock. People still carry and place the items. Software only helps with the counting and planning step.
Automated PAR-room systems record usage and trigger restocking with no manual counts, but they do not physically restock shelves or carts.
Linen and supply carts are refilled every day to set quotas. This is hands-on work that takes physical presence in storage rooms and on carts.

Under OSHA directive CPL 2-1.36, workers climbing communication towers must use a fall arrest system (1926.502) or a ladder safety device (1926.1053(a)), and they must be trained. This is a physical task that a person has to do in harness.

Drones can cut down on climbs for inspections, but the tower erectors' association (NATE) and AT&T say drones cannot do rigging, antenna work or line work. Climbers are still needed, and drones are not software agents anyway.
Drone-based digital twins can reduce the need to climb for site audits, but they do not climb towers to reach components. They are also robotic hardware, which the reference agent does not have.
Beam AI says its compliance agents gather ESG data, flag policy gaps and produce disclosures for SFDR and similar frameworks. This is a vendor claim and has not been independently checked.

ESGAgent.ai says it automates sustainability compliance, including tracking EU Taxonomy and SEC climate-rule changes and reporting aligned to GRI, SASB and TCFD. This is company-reported in trade news.
Compliance & Risks markets AI-native sustainability compliance intelligence that monitors regulations. The task is digital oversight work that needs no physical presence or professional licence.
Kentucky law says no one may install, erect or repair boilers without a state license, and getting one requires passing an exam.
Michigan licenses boiler installers in classes based on boiler size and type, and an applicant needs at least 5 years of installation experience.

Installing a boiler is physical on-site work: rigging and moving a heavy vessel, leveling it so the water-level controls and steam separation work properly, and fitting seismic restraints. An agent can only help with document steps such as reading the manual or planning, which take up little of the task's time.

Google DeepMind's Aletheia (arXiv 2602.10177, March 2026) is described as a mathematics research agent that works end to end in natural language. Its authors say it produced several papers of publishable quality, one of them with no human intervention. These are the authors' own claims and have not been checked independently.

ICMJE, COPE and the major publishers say AI tools cannot be authors because authorship requires being accountable for the work. Human authors stay responsible for all content and must disclose any AI use. This summary comes from secondary sources, not the ICMJE or COPE documents themselves.

COPE's position, as quoted on a journal's authorship page, is that AI cannot take responsibility for a submitted work, declare conflicts of interest, or handle copyright and licence agreements. This is a secondhand quote.

Hotel guests can already book vetted, background-checked babysitters for their room through an online app (Sitters UK), with bookings from 2 hours and arrival in as little as 90 minutes. The booking part of the task is fully digital.

Agencies like Aunty.sg match a vetted sitter for in-room hotel care and email the sitter's details, reviews and references. An agent could handle the request, matching and confirmation by web or email, but a parent's trust in the choice of caregiver usually rests on the concierge's own vetted agency relationships and personal judgement.

Voice and AI agents can already answer questions, take bookings and send confirmations for babysitting services. I found no turnkey AI concierge that books and vouches for childcare from start to finish, so a human still reviews the choice of sitter and gives the guest the final assurance.

Vendors describe AI data-entry agents that run the whole pipeline: they take in email and uploads, extract data into a schema, validate it and write it to a CRM, ERP or spreadsheet. Cases where the agent is unsure still go to a human, which supports L2 rather than L3.

Airtable's Omni builds base structure and field agents, and its field agents fill in cell data automatically. Tools connected over MCP, such as Claude, can create and edit fields. This covers both creating a database and entering data into it.
Airtable runs a developer page aimed at agents, so agents can reach databases through software access alone. No physical presence is needed.

The Cabrillo National Monument visitor center SOP lists physical opening steps: unlocking doors, updating the passport stamp dates and filling in a whiteboard with the date, tide times, scheduled programs, groups due in and the weather forecast.

The Lookout visitor centre closing checklist covers turning off equipment and lights, lowering the blind, locking up, bringing in the flag and collection box, logging the shift, cleaning, and a radio announcement that the site is closing.

General facility opening and closing guidance includes a perimeter security check, disarming and setting alarms, starting lighting and HVAC, checking the cash float, reconciling cash and locking doors. These are mostly physical steps. An agent could only help with digital parts like workstation startup, shift logs and status updates.

EarthCam Control Center 9 uses AI on jobsite cameras to report usage of 50+ equipment and vehicle types, detect 85+ types of equipment and materials and their status, and flag labor utilization issues. An agent could watch these feeds remotely, but only where such systems are installed.

Telematics shows machine and operator productivity, but a Dodge study found only 17% of contractors use technology that monitors operator behavior. Most field monitoring is still done in person by the supervisor.

OSHA's excavation rule requires a competent person to inspect the site daily and to have authority to take prompt corrective action. Courts have held that this must be a human with real power to stop work, and it is often the foreman.
I couldn't verify anything online. The search tool returned an API error, so this rating is based only on what I already know about the task.

Setting up equipment for site testing means physically moving, placing, connecting and calibrating instruments such as soil probes, sensors, sampling gear and lab apparatus. An AI agent with no body can't do this. It can only help with planning, checklists, setup instructions and configuring the software or data loggers.
I don't know of any licence or law that requires a human to sign off on this routine setup work in typical jurisdictions.

In state electronic death registration systems, the funeral home starts the death record and picks the physician. The physician then logs in from anywhere to enter the cause of death and sign, and gets email alerts for records waiting on them. Clerks can update the record but cannot sign it, so an agent can start and chase the record but the licensed certifier has to sign.

When a certifier is not online, funeral or clinic staff print an attestation form, get the certifier to sign it, and fax it into the system. Some cases still involve paper handling and getting signatures by hand.

Insurance assignment services connected to Passare pull case data automatically, generate the assignment paperwork, submit claims electronically and talk to insurers. The family still has to sign the assignment, and the vendor acts under a limited power of attorney.

Commercial workforce platforms advertise AI agents that assign shifts automatically by availability and skills, reschedule after absences, fill open shifts and flag labor-rule problems. These are vendor claims, not independent tests.
Fraunhofer IKS and ATOSS built a reinforcement-learning shift-planning agent that automates hospital staff scheduling, so the core scheduling step can be handed to an agent.

Predictive-scheduling laws such as Oregon's set rules for how far ahead schedules must be posted and for premium pay when they change. They do not require a human to write or sign the schedule, and posting can be electronic.
Parts counter job postings list keeping the department and work area orderly, neat and clean, and stocking shelves, as hands-on duties done in the store or warehouse.

Employees may be given a section of the showroom or storage area to keep clean, stocked and orderly. This is physical work that software-only agents without robotics cannot do. They could at most make cleaning checklists or schedules, which is a small share of the time.
Housekeeping in a parts counter area is a general workplace duty. Typical jurisdictions do not require a licence or a human signature for it.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451(f)(7), a competent person must supervise and direct anyone who erects, moves, dismantles or alters a scaffold. A competent person must also check the scaffold for visible defects before each shift, which requires someone on site.

Scaffold planning software such as Avontus Scaffold Designer and Layher LayPLAN can generate layouts, tie and bracing plans, and parts lists automatically. This only touches the planning sub-step. Someone still has to put up the scaffold by hand.
softtech's scaffmax models a building and fills it with scaffolding wall by wall, accounting for ground conditions. It produces plans and material lists, not the physical assembly.

In 2026, an MCP-based agent workflow connected to EnergyPlus cut energy-model inspection and modification tasks from 1-2 hours to under 15 minutes, and an agentic mode automated parametric analysis. The authors say professionals should stay in charge of decisions.

UMD's Rapid Energy Auditor produces a preliminary audit from utility data alone and flags which facilities need a follow-up onsite assessment. This shows the analysis part of advising can be automated, while site-specific data still depends on people visiting the building.

Programs such as Energize Denver require audits and recommendations from credentialed third parties (a licensed PE, AEE CEM/CEA or ASHRAE BEAP) following ASHRAE Standard 211 Level 2, so a human remains accountable for formal advice.

Zenoti salon software tracks stock from sales and how much product services use. It flags products that reach a reorder level, can create purchase orders automatically and stores supplier details so orders go out from the system. This covers the ordering sub-step from start to finish. Source is vendor marketing, not independently checked.

Meevo builds purchase orders automatically from stock levels and usage rates before items run out. An agent with computer use could run this and send orders with no one stepping in. Source is vendor marketing, not independently checked.

Salon inventory guidance still assumes in-person stock counts (audits), and these software estimates are reset against those counts. Setting up retail displays, restocking shelves and storing backbar products are physical jobs that an agent without a body cannot do. No licence or sign-off is needed to order supplies.

Under BLM policy, the authorized officer (a human official) sets priorities for NEPA and other legal requirements before grazing permits are issued. Renewal needs a finding that the permittee has a satisfactory performance record, and the officer must consult with permittees and the public, so a human has to sign and stay accountable.
BLM renewals check each allotment against rangeland health standards, which depends on monitoring data collected in the field.

Satellite and AI tools such as Enriched Ag Insights, the Rangeland Analysis Platform and GrassSignal already produce stocking recommendations, recovery periods, overgrazing estimates and rotation plans. An agent could handle the analysis, planning and paperwork, but field compliance checks and work with ranchers in person still need a human.
Glaze chemistry software such as Insight-Live and Glazy can calculate recipes and batches. This is the only digital part of the task that an AI could help with.
Spray glazing is done by hand with HVLP spray guns in a ventilated booth, using a turntable and a respirator. The person has to judge glaze thickness and keep the strokes even.
Glaze is applied by physically handling the pieces through dipping, pouring, brushing or spraying. It takes a lot of practice to get an even coat.

Interact's 2026 release added agentic tools: one lets communicators ask questions about engagement data in plain language, and an Executive Assistant Agent sorts employee tasks by priority. This covers the analytics sub-steps of internal relations.
Lyzr sells an AI Internal Communication Agent that summarizes announcements and tracks employee engagement and sentiment. Its claimed results are the vendor's own marketing figures.

A vendor blog cites survey data saying 52% of internal-comms practitioners use AI at least weekly. It frames the buyer's question as who reviews what the agent sends to employees, which means a human still reviews the output. This is a vendor source, so I treat it as opinion.

Microsoft's Copilot onboarding uses a 'Learning Agent' that walks users through role-tailored practice tasks in about 10 to 15 minutes. AI can tutor the person, but the human still has to do the learning.
Vendors such as VisualSP sell in-app, in-context AI guidance so employees can learn new tools while they work. This speeds up human learning step by step rather than replacing it.

Microsoft Learn's onboarding guidance for organisations relies on training strategies, champion programmes and rapid-enablement training of people. The human's own skill-building is the essential output.

Vendor material describes AI agents for manufacturing that find recurring OEE drops and create improvement tasks on their own, and that do predictive maintenance and OEE optimization. This means the analysis and recommendation steps can be delegated when the plant's data systems are connected. The performance figures are vendor claims and have not been independently checked.

OSHA puts safety duties on the employer, such as checking workplace conditions and keeping equipment safe. Plant manager job postings make the manager responsible for OSHA compliance across plant operations. So putting cost changes into practice requires human accountability and on-site checking.

Environmental permit documents such as Title V and NPDES must be signed and certified by a human responsible official or an authorized representative. An agent cannot be the one who certifies regulatory compliance.

SAP Transportation Management reportedly has AI agents that plan, run and optimise shipments on their own, from route planning to resolving problems as they happen. That covers the main sub-steps of comparing routing and carrier options.

Agents described in industry sources handle multimodal routing and freight-rate negotiation using live market data. Survey data citing Trimble says 31% of carriers and logistics providers use AI for route planning, and poor data quality (57%) is the top barrier.

BCG reports that AI in logistics often fails to deliver ROI because of data and integration problems. This supports keeping a human to check assumptions and approve the financial impact analysis before it is used.

Vendor products such as Fountain's AI Recruiter (Anna) and Interviewer.AI already run structured first-round screening interviews for high-volume frontline and warehouse hiring and score the answers. A human team still reviews the results before deciding (the efficiency figures are vendor claims).

Interviewer.AI markets AI video interviews built specifically for hiring warehouse workers and claims a large cut in recruiter time on first-round screening. This is a self-reported, unverified figure.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l), forklift operator training must include hands-on practical training and an in-person evaluation on the site's own equipment. Online material can cover only the classroom part, so much of the training needs a human trainer on site.

Current security-architecture guidance and products cover designing integrated control layers (identity, access control, data governance, enforcement points). This is the kind of design and integration recommendation an agent can research and draft. Vendors still advise keeping AI advisory, with humans reviewing decisions in mission-critical physical security settings.

Physical security integration recommendations depend on site- and system-specific factors such as video availability, door access, incident response and operational continuity. Getting that information usually takes site knowledge and access to client systems, which a human typically provides and verifies.

Licensing for low-voltage security design varies by state. California, for example, requires a C-7 licence for CCTV design and a C-28 licence for access control installation by the contracting entity, while several states have no statewide licence. Advisory recommendations by themselves are generally not required to be signed by a licence holder.

Esri describes agentic mapping apps where a user asks a plain-language question and the agent picks and runs the spatial analysis tools, then returns results. Its ArcGIS Pro assistant, which can generate ArcPy and Arcade code, is still in beta, so map-and-layer production can be partly delegated.

A USGS presentation shows Esri's AI assistants for Pro, Survey123 and Arcade code generation still at Preview or Beta stage in 2026, so a human still has to review cartographic quality and data correctness.

A surveyor's seal is required only for survey products such as plats and boundary maps. General-purpose GIS maps, tables and reports usually need no licensed sign-off, though some states define surveying broadly.

Chesapeake Conservancy reports that its deep-learning model maps wetlands at 1-metre resolution with 94% accuracy. It still needs local training data from state wetland inventories and the National Wetlands Inventory (NWI), so automated mapping covers a large part of determining wetland extent from existing data.

A 2025 practitioner presentation says AI wetland-probability layers are being added to the NWI update process, but their boundaries do not consistently match NWI standards. A human expert therefore still has to review and correct the output.

Regulators such as the Corps and state agencies make the final call on wetland boundaries and verify delineations by consultants. That formal step applies to regulatory delineation, not to compiling or interpreting biodata for planning.

AI script-breakdown tools such as Filmustage and RivetAI can find and tag props, costumes, wardrobe, locations, vehicles and other production elements, and link them to schedules and budgets. That covers the 'identify' part of the task from start to finish, but the breakdowns still need human review for accuracy and creative fit.

Approval is a creative authority held by the director: production guidelines say the director gives final approval on props, and scenic elements must satisfy the director and production designer before tech rehearsal. In practice, sets, fittings and lighting are often reviewed in person.

Production policies set the director's prop list and approval deadlines inside an internal workflow run by people. These are institutional rules, not legal ones, so no licence or law requires a human to sign.
Jotform's Copywriter Intake AI Agent template runs conversational intake with clients. It gathers project details and brand information and accepts uploaded brand guidelines.
Monday.com's creative brief agent builds briefs from Slack threads and voice-note transcripts. It states its assumptions where information is missing and flags conflicting stakeholder feedback.
Jasper's Creative Brief Agent organizes goals, audiences and deliverables into a brief for stakeholders and applies the user's brand voice settings.

Under NWCG, the Cost Unit Leader gathers incident cost data, runs obligation reports from the ICARS database, builds cost reports and charts, analyzes cost-effectiveness and recommends savings. These are data and reporting steps that an agent with system access could carry out.

Line officers, agency administrators and incident commanders must review costs daily and document those reviews. Unresolved cost concerns go to the Agency Administrator or Line Officer, so a human holds the accountability for deciding whether spending is necessary.

Incident business follows the NWCG SIIBM (PMS 902), and federal expenditures of $10M or more trigger formal cost reviews. These rules give an agent clear criteria to check spending against, but delegated authority and sign-off stay with people.
