Fire alarm testing is usually done in person: designated inspectors walk the whole building, set off each device and log pass or fail. Self-test detectors and cloud platforms such as Honeywell CLSS cover only some devices and work through the vendor's own systems.
NFPA 25 allows automatic or remote inspection and testing only through electronic devices installed for that purpose. Everything else (valves, sprinklers, pumps, extinguishers) needs someone on site.
NFPA 25 requires inspection, testing and maintenance (ITM) work to be done by qualified personnel. The local fire authority (AHJ) decides what training, certification or licence each ITM task needs.

A vendor (DocsBot) markets an AI agent trained on a security company's post orders, SOPs and client instructions. It answers guards' questions and sends issues that need judgment to a human supervisor, so the written explanation step can be automated.
General HR policy agents already explain company policies to employees from the uploaded documents and cite the source, with no human answering each question.

Security guard licensing is set state by state and covers guard training and registration. The search found no state rule requiring a licensed human to personally explain company policies. Supervisor duties such as giving direction and motivating staff are set by employers.

Guard tour software already checks guard compliance automatically. It records timestamped checkpoint scans (NFC, QR, GPS, RFID) tied to each guard's badge, and sends alerts when a tour starts late, ends early or misses a checkpoint. An agent can review this data and report on it without a human.
Patrols are linked to the guard's badge login and the data syncs automatically, so the digital record of each guard's adherence is available to software.

Guard licensing is set state by state, with no federal license, and no separate licence tier for supervisors was found. That suggests no legal rule requires a human to do the monitoring, but on-site observation, coaching and corrective action still depend on being there in person.

Salvage means hands-on work at the fire scene: pumping out basements, draining water pooled in ceilings, covering contents with salvage covers, and sealing broken windows and doors with plastic sheeting.
Salvage activities include expelling smoke, controlling runoff, removing water, and covering broken windows and doors, all carried out by crews on site.
Crews remove smoke by physically ventilating the building and keep ventilating during overhaul; the building's HVAC system is usually shut off rather than used.

AI camera systems such as Rekor's Argos Guardian combine radar, video and AI plate reading to flag violations and build citation evidence packets. These systems sit outside the agent and only cover detecting and documenting violations. They do not drive a patrol or make arrests.
A July 2026 NCSL/CDT report says AI-upgraded license plate readers are now used to pick which vehicles to pull over. Officers still have to make the physical stop.
Arizona AG opinion: only a POST-certified peace officer can exercise the authority to detain and arrest. A non-certified person has no more authority than any citizen.

AI agents for skip tracing are sold to law enforcement (ICE has contracted vendors whose AI agents locate people and map their associates), so the search-and-locate part can be sped up. The arrest itself still has to be carried out by people.
In California, arrest warrants are addressed to peace officers, and only the officers or authorized public employees who receive the warrant can carry it out.
In Louisiana, only a peace officer with authority in the place where the person is found can execute an arrest warrant.

Jail management systems already speed up booking. Kologik says arrestee data syncs automatically from CAD and RMS. SmartJAIL can import arrest and charging reports to fill in cases, charges and bond details. This makes the records side digital, but a person still runs the system.

CentralSquare says automated intake cuts booking from about 45 to 15 minutes per inmate. This is a vendor claim. The physical steps still need a person on site: searching the arrestee, taking prints, photos and property, and keeping custody.
Booking still involves capturing fingerprints in person with livescan devices linked to criminal-justice databases such as FBI/AFIS. Some agencies still fill out hard-copy forms by hand.

Wheelchair securement is a hands-on job. Staff position the chair, center it between the floor tracks, lock the brakes and attach the straps. The bus must not move until the chair is fully and properly tied down.
District procedure says two adults should take part in loading and unloading. The bus driver or bus aide is responsible for making sure the student and equipment are secured before the bus moves.

Guidance requires a 4-point tie-down with a separate occupant restraint, following the manufacturers' instructions. Staff must not improvise a securement. This is physical work with nothing an AI agent can do through software.

The Ontario MTO bus handbook says the backing spotter must stand behind the bus where the driver can see them in the mirror. Without a spotter, the driver must leave the bus and check the path. The task requires someone physically there, outside the vehicle.
Industry guidance recommends an adult outside the bus to help with backing. Backup alarms and cameras are presented as extra measures that do not replace that person.

Help for drivers when backing up comes from cameras, mirror monitors and radar sensors built into the bus. These are hardware systems, not general-purpose AI agents that a monitor could reach through software, so an agent cannot see the rear of the bus or signal the driver.
Wendy's FreshAI voice ordering is expanding to up to 600 restaurants and reportedly handled about 86% of drive-thru orders without staff stepping in. The remaining orders were passed to human staff.

A May 2026 vendor blog (a possibly biased source) reports AI drive-thru order accuracy of about 83%, against 87% for human-taken orders, rising to 95% when staff help. Yum!/Taco Bell has used voice AI on millions of orders, and McDonald's ended its pilot over order errors. Human review and correction are still needed.

Square released a quick-service kiosk in October 2026 with a voice layer that understands the menu. Vendors say systems like this send orders to the POS and kitchen display systems and print order numbers or stubs, so no hands-on ticket writing is needed.
Cash recyclers in casino cages are hardware that accepts, validates, stores and dispenses cash, and they handle bill breaking. This automation is physical machinery, not a software AI agent.

Glory sells cage recyclers and self-service kiosks that count, authenticate and dispense notes and coins for buy-ins and payouts. Doing this without a person to handle the cash takes dedicated physical hardware.
In this patented cage method, a cashier chooses the denomination and quantity and the recycler dispenses it. Software only sends the order, and handing the cash to the customer stays a physical job.

Vendor blogs describe AI agents that watch for rule changes, collect evidence, propose edits to policy and procedure documents, send them for review and keep an audit trail. A named person still accepts, changes or rejects each edit. These are vendor claims and have not been checked independently.

Agentic AI tools for managing standard operating procedures are said to draft, update and send out revised procedures when requirements change. A human review step is still recommended. This is also a vendor claim.
One guide says generative AI can do up to 80% of the work of updating policy documents, with a human expert doing the final review. The guide gives no independent evidence for this figure.

Commercial APIs from vendors such as Middesk, CRS (sourced from LexisNexis) and D&B already return liens, judgments and bankruptcies for underwriting, so the core lookups can be automated. These are vendor marketing pages, not independent checks.

Court-record API coverage is patchy. Cobalt's Court Records API covers only New York State and Miami-Dade County, so some places still need manual searches of county portals or courthouses, and a person has to confirm the records match the right applicant.

The FCRA requires a permissible purpose and reasonable procedures for maximum possible accuracy, especially for criminal records. These sources did not show any law requiring a human to do the search or sign it, but mistakes create liability, which supports a human review step.

Commercial aquaculture farm-management platforms keep a daily fish or shrimp inventory with egg-to-harvest traceability tied to regulatory reporting. That means an agent could do the record-keeping, reconciliation and reporting digitally.

ERP and Odoo aquaculture modules link fish batches from hatchery to dispatch, along with harvest grading, stock entries and sales invoices. Records of fish sold and shipped can therefore be generated automatically from transaction data.

State rules require stocking receipts listing date, species, length and number stocked, signed and dated by the hatchery. The counts come from physical observation on site, and a human signature is needed, but the rules do not require a licensed professional.

Digital training in aquaculture is mostly VR simulation. One fish-farm VR and photogrammetry project stopped at proof-of-concept and said the technology 'requires further development'. That means hands-on training is still mostly done in person, though an agent could write the materials.

Under OSHA, employers must train tractor and farm-equipment operators when they start the job and at least once a year after that, on safe operating practices. The source I found does not say a licensed trainer is needed. However, the training covers equipment on the farm, which points to in-person demonstration.

University farm safety programs require supervisors to keep records of training dates, the trainer, the topics covered and the equipment each worker is certified to run. An agent could do this kind of paperwork, but the practical training and certification happen on site.

Sawmill software such as Tally-I/O tracks log and lumber inventory, production and yard management with barcode scanning. An agent could use these records to match logs in storage to production needs and transport schedules, then send out the selection and movement plan.
Yard and dock scheduling systems let dispatchers plan loading and unloading against shipments and yard space, and let carriers book appointments. This covers the scheduling part of the task.

No product turned up for log merchandising, meaning checking log grade, condition and species on site. Log-yard records are often patchy, and the loader operators have to be directed in the yard. So a human is still needed on the ground to confirm the selection and supervise the moves, and no law or licence requires a human sign-off.
Nursery management software (Tend) says it lets growers build production plans and automatically sync inventory updates with the crop plan and customer orders.
Mprise Agriware's ERP for growers advertises AI (Copilot) that generates orders and automates sales-order entry.

Folio3's nursery software claims to assign, track and optimize field and greenhouse tasks by crop stage, crew and work zone. An agent can turn orders and inventory into a task list, but a supervisor still has to check it against crop readiness, weather and crew that day.

Equipment checkout software for agricultural clients records inspections and signatures at each check-in and check-out. Software handles the logging, but a person still has to hand over and take back the equipment.
Tool crib systems record which worker took which tool and when it is due back, using barcodes on both tools and employees. Scanning and handover are still done in person.

Tool crib software can check out tools against a specific technician's work assignments, so an AI could plan the issue lists and track returns. It cannot move or inspect physical implements, ladders or containers.
onX Hunt's private-land data usually lists the landowner's name, mailing address and property boundaries. An agent could do the research step of finding who to contact.

Online permission forms, such as Typeform's template, collect the hunter's details, dates and a liability acknowledgment, and can be sent by email or link. An agent could draft them and handle the paperwork.

In Tennessee, the landowner issues the written permission slip and the hunter carries it. The landowner is the one who signs, so no law requires the hunter to sign anything personally. Getting a yes still depends mostly on building trust with the landowner, often face to face.
Fishing hands cast and lower nets, pots, lines and traps into the water, attach running gear and bait, and set lines into position by hand on deck.
Longline deployment is done on deck with machinery, under a supervisor's instructions, using floats, dan poles and weights so the gear does not foul. This is physical seamanship work.

Automatic baiting and setting machines such as Mustad Autoline are vessel-mounted mechanical systems that crew run on board. They are not software agents, so a non-embodied AI agent cannot do the deployment.

Weathernews' SeaNavigator for Master is an onboard AI tool for ship captains. It reads wave and wind forecasts, grounding risk and route simulations, and suggests route changes. A human meteorologist still checks its suggestions in fast-changing storms, and the sources show no use in fishing fleets.

SOLAS Regulation 34-1 and ISM Code section 5.2 give the master overriding authority and responsibility for safety decisions, including how to handle heavy weather. Commercial weather routeing advice does not replace the master's decision.

Heavy-weather practice expects the master to change course and speed as good seamanship requires, based on what is observed on board. Judging the vessel's condition means being physically present to watch sea state, stability, icing and gear.
